components.text: Whether the affirmative's probability-raising considerations supply recognizable evidence sufficient for the motion.
The affirmative must warrant its claimed probability increase with recognizable evidence rather than merely define it.
Whether ordinary probability-raising considerations warrant belief in the extraordinary hypothesis of an infinitely powerful divine intelligence.
A probability-raising definition does not alone show that the offered facts adequately warrant an extraordinary divine hypothesis.
Whether philosophical objections to actual infinity adequately support the premise that the universe began to exist.
The philosophical case against an infinite past cannot rest on classical absurdity intuitions when mathematics and physics successfully use infinities.
Whether unexplained contingent existence licenses an inference to God rather than continued investigation of possible physical explanations.
Presently unknown physical explanations do not license an inference from contingency to God.
Whether the universe's beginning requires a divine first cause when an eternal multiverse could generate our local universe.
An eternal inflationary multiverse would block the inference from our universe's beginning to a relevant divine first cause.
Whether morality originates in God if an independently wrong act would remain wrong even under divine approval.
If moral wrongness constrains what God could approve, objective morality is not explained by divine choice.
Whether quantum-vacuum and multiverse cosmology can be past-eternal and thereby avoid an ultimate cosmic beginning.
Whether mathematical handling of infinity answers the objection to an actually instantiated infinite past.
Quantum-vacuum and inflationary cosmologies do not establish a past-eternal physical state.
Mathematical manipulation of infinity does not show that an actual infinite temporal history exists.
Whether physical dynamics, varied laws, and observer selection can explain apparent fine-tuning without supernatural design.
Physical processes, varied laws, and observer selection can account for apparent fine-tuning without supernatural design.
Whether many-worlds and observer selection explain embodied interactive observers without relocating fine-tuning to multiverse-generating laws.
A multiverse must explain embodied observers and the special laws governing universe production rather than merely multiply worlds.
Whether divine morality is arbitrary when commands necessarily express God's compassionate, just, and fair character.
Necessary expressions of God's essentially compassionate and just character prevent arbitrary immoral commands.
Whether moral understanding and decent conduct require belief in or ontological dependence upon a necessarily good God.
Whether rationality, evolution, and biology can make morality intelligible without a divine foundation.
Moral understanding and conduct can arise through rationality, evolution, and biology without belief in God.
Atheists' continued moral conduct challenges the claim that morality depends practically on belief in God.
Whether known dynamics and the uncertain life-relevance of vacuum energy undermine fine-tuning as evidence of competent purpose.
Whether unexplained features of cosmology establish purposive multiverse-level design.
Known dynamics explain some alleged tuning, and the remaining vacuum-energy value is not shown to be intentionally life-directed.
Residual ignorance about a value does not establish design or purposeful multiverse laws.
Whether anecdotal human testimony makes error more plausible than resurrection as an explanation of the reported historical claims.
Anecdotal historical testimony is more likely to contain human error than to establish a miraculous resurrection.
Whether imagination, illusion, error, or deliberate intervention more plausibly explain resurrection reports than a supernatural event.
Imagination, illusion, or deliberate intervention are ordinary explanations more plausible than supernatural resurrection.
The proposed ordinary rivals must account for the affirmative's complete three-fact set.
Whether ordinary rival accounts jointly explain the accepted historical facts with adequate scope, power, plausibility, and non-ad-hocness.
Whether general testimonial fallibility defeats the specific comparative historical case.
Naturalistic rivals fail explanatory scope, power, plausibility, and non-ad-hocness when applied to the accepted historical facts.
Generic testimonial error does not furnish a specific explanation with adequate scope for the cited facts.
Whether explanatory inquiry stops arbitrarily at God or principledly at a being whose existence is necessary by nature.
Stopping with a necessary being is principled because only contingent entities require external causes.
A merely eternal multiverse does not thereby possess necessity in its own nature.
Whether God has any demonstrated explanatory advantage over an eternal, physically motivated multiverse as the necessary terminus.
Whether the necessary explanatory ground must be divine rather than a natural multiverse.
Defining God as necessary has no shown advantage over treating a physically motivated eternal multiverse as the terminus.
The affirmative must justify why the necessary explanation is divine rather than natural.
Whether rational evidence must be restricted to scientific or empirical proof when that restriction is not itself scientifically provable.
Whether a broad cumulative hypothesis may be assessed through moral, philosophical, historical, and scientific considerations.
The legitimate demand is rationally warranted evidence, not an exclusive restriction to scientific proof.
A broad cumulative case can include moral, philosophical, historical, and scientific considerations while still requiring adequate warrants.
Theism's claimed advantage must be assessed across the full explanatory range rather than cosmology alone.
